title: Show a skill
subject: Careers
label: Public edition
objective_verbatim: Choose evidence of one skill and explain how it could fit a job.
display_objective: Choose work that shows a skill. Link it to a job.
approved_activity: Review actual work from the earlier lessons and select an example that shows a skill. Match it to a fictional role, practise explaining the link and choose one next step.
where_this_leads: This helps me explain what I can do and what I want to learn.
unit: Working with others and showing a skill
unit_status: new descriptive grouping for this pair; no qualification unit title inferred
calendar_note: Year A. 7–11 December 2026. One 40-minute lesson; no day or clock slot inferred. Week 7 is assessing.

thread_tags.rationale: S: reflect on a contribution, skill or next step. So: listen, pass work on and explain a link. IL: choose a response mode, pause or support. MR: respect each contribution and allow time.

evidence.description: A skill-and-evidence card, a job-role match and a next step; missing work remains clearly marked.

routes.Supported: Review up to two pieces of the learner’s actual earlier work with an adult. Choose one, select a skill and fictional role card, and use a sentence stem to explain the link. Record prompts.
routes.Independent: Choose actual earlier work, identify one skill it shows and explain how that skill could help a task on a fictional role card. Choose a specific next step.
routes.Aspire: Compare two possible examples, explain which supports the claim more clearly, and name a limit or further evidence needed. Choose a next step that addresses that gap.

Prepare each learner’s actual work or specific observation records from Weeks 1–5, including Week 5 if available. Keep adult models in a separate folder marked MODEL. Print the two evidence pages and three support pages for each learner. Do not invent missing work or use another learner’s work. Year A · Autumn 2 Week 6: 7–11 December 2026. One 40-minute lesson; no day or clock slot is inferred. This lesson is formative. Week 7 is assessing.
This helps me explain what I can do and what I want to learn.

A supports the claim: actual work and a precise observation show the skill and its link to the role. B is an unsupported claim; C is someone else’s work. Ask the learner to point to the part of their selected work that supports the skill. If it does not support that skill, revise the claim or choose a different example. Do not infer a skill from a job picture alone.
Supported: Review up to two pieces of the learner’s actual earlier work with an adult. Choose one, select a skill and fictional role card, and use a sentence stem to explain the link. Record prompts.
Independent: Choose actual earlier work, identify one skill it shows and explain how that skill could help a task on a fictional role card. Choose a specific next step.
Aspire: Compare two possible examples, explain which supports the claim more clearly, and name a limit or further evidence needed. Choose a next step that addresses that gap.

Use four minutes to look at actual earlier work and choose an example. Use five minutes to link the observed skill to a task on one fictional role card and practise the explanation to an adult. Use three minutes to choose a next step. If the example is missing, record the gap and a plan to recover it. A brief new task may be recorded as new work, never as recovered earlier evidence.

Use fictional unnamed jobs, employers and settings. Use large paper cards on a clear table; adults prepare cutting. No machinery, lifting or real workplace task is needed. Do not ask about body, family or private experiences. Allow an adult partner, a quiet response, a communication aid or a pause. Learners can query unclear or unsafe instructions. Follow the setting’s usual route if a concern is raised.

Keep a specific work reference and date, what the example actually shows, one skill, the chosen fictional role and task, the learner’s explanation of the link, and one next step. Record support and the adult’s reply. Mark missing, unclear or unverified evidence explicitly. A role match is a teaching judgement, not proof of job readiness or qualification completion.

Use VF · WS · I · NS+ (Yellow Box) · // self-edit · ? read back · R responded · E evidence in the evidence record. R requires Voice, Audience, a specific NS+ prompt and the learner response in their own colour. E is recorded only when actual work is banked. Record support and unfinished work. Blank forms and adult models are not learner evidence.

Space: calm seating and clear resources. Voice: choose a response mode, explain a choice or request help. Audience: an adult listens, replies and allows time. Influence: record any change to support or the next task in response.

S: reflect on a contribution, skill or next step. So: listen, hand work on and explain a link to another person. IL: choose a response mode and request a pause or support. MR: allow each person time, acknowledge their contribution and avoid ridicule.

Offer the learner’s actual explanation of the work-to-role link to the Communication portfolio. Record who listened, their reply and the learner’s response. Staff confirm any mapping from the evidence.

A supports the claim: actual work and a precise observation show the skill and its link to the role. B is an unsupported claim; C is someone else’s work. Ask the learner to point to the part of their selected work that supports the skill. If it does not support that skill, revise the claim or choose a different example. Do not infer a skill from a job picture alone.
Supported: Review up to two pieces of the learner’s actual earlier work with an adult. Choose one, select a skill and fictional role card, and use a sentence stem to explain the link. Record prompts.
Independent: Choose actual earlier work, identify one skill it shows and explain how that skill could help a task on a fictional role card. Choose a specific next step.
Aspire: Compare two possible examples, explain which supports the claim more clearly, and name a limit or further evidence needed. Choose a next step that addresses that gap.

Use four minutes to look at actual earlier work and choose an example. Use five minutes to link the observed skill to a task on one fictional role card and practise the explanation to an adult. Use three minutes to choose a next step. If the example is missing, record the gap and a plan to recover it. A brief new task may be recorded as new work, never as recovered earlier evidence.

Use fictional unnamed jobs, employers and settings. Use large paper cards on a clear table; adults prepare cutting. No machinery, lifting or real workplace task is needed. Do not ask about body, family or private experiences. Allow an adult partner, a quiet response, a communication aid or a pause. Learners can query unclear or unsafe instructions. Follow the setting’s usual route if a concern is raised.

Keep a specific work reference and date, what the example actually shows, one skill, the chosen fictional role and task, the learner’s explanation of the link, and one next step. Record support and the adult’s reply. Mark missing, unclear or unverified evidence explicitly. A role match is a teaching judgement, not proof of job readiness or qualification completion.

Use VF · WS · I · NS+ (Yellow Box) · // self-edit · ? read back · R responded · E evidence in the evidence record. R requires Voice, Audience, a specific NS+ prompt and the learner response in their own colour. E is recorded only when actual work is banked. Record support and unfinished work. Blank forms and adult models are not learner evidence.

Space: calm seating and clear resources. Voice: choose a response mode, explain a choice or request help. Audience: an adult listens, replies and allows time. Influence: record any change to support or the next task in response.

S: reflect on a contribution, skill or next step. So: listen, hand work on and explain a link to another person. IL: choose a response mode and request a pause or support. MR: allow each person time, acknowledge their contribution and avoid ridicule.

Offer the learner’s actual explanation of the work-to-role link to the Communication portfolio. Record who listened, their reply and the learner’s response. Staff confirm any mapping from the evidence.

paragraphs: These are teaching guides. Record the learner’s actual response and support. The roles and settings are fictional and unnamed.

Use only the fictional model on Support Cards page 2. The model worker sorted three circles and two squares into the right groups; an adult observed the action. The skill is sorting by shape. This could help the stock helper sort paper cards. A next step is to count each group and record the totals. This model teaches the link and must not be filed as a learner’s work.

A supports the claim: actual work and a precise observation show the skill and its link to the role. B is an unsupported claim; C is someone else’s work. Valid links depend on the actual work: accurate shape grouping may support the stock helper role; a recorded two-step packing sequence may support the packer role; a clear observed handover may support the team helper role. More than one reasoned match can be valid. Checking the pack does not prove independent counting unless counting was observed. A copied model or blank form is not learner evidence.

Liking a job does not by itself show a skill. An adult model shows how to explain, not what the learner has done. A learner may describe help they used and still identify a skill. A gap is a reason to plan the next step, not a reason to invent a record.

Follow the setting’s usual route if a concern is raised.
